item.title: Led by Trump, Republicans Close Midterms With Ugly Personal Attacks
item.description:
In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a vulnerable Republican, baselessly said his Democratic opponent “probably is grooming” children.

In Texas, Republicans have cast James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, as a “freak” and insinuated he is gay, secretly a vegan, and obsessed with transgender children because he made statements supporting them in the past.

And in Michigan, Republicans have targeted the Democratic Senate nominee, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, with Islamophobic attacks. Mr. Trump has described Dr. El-Sayed as a “vicious, violent jihadist.”

Facing a backlash over rising prices and working to overcome the president’s deep unpopularity, Republicans across the country have tarred their opponents with false, inflammatory and deeply personal attacks in the final stretch of the midterm election.

In many cases, they are following the lead of a president who has repeatedly rewritten the rules of acceptable discourse in American politics. Many of the attacks have drawn little pushback from within the party, but some Republicans say they are concerned by the trend.

“It’s awful,” said former Senator Jeff Flake, an Arizona Republican and critic of Mr. Trump. Mr. Flake, who is backing candidates in both parties in the midterms, said Republicans had gone down a darker road in their messaging: “We’ve gotten progressively more crass and crude and vulgar. But this seems to be a new level.”

The strategy risks turning off some moderate voters who see the rhetoric as over-the-top or offensive, political observers said. But it could be effective at energizing the Republican base. Democrats, who have widely condemned the Republicans’ attacks, worry the lines will land with some voters.

Democrats themselves have at times used strikingly personal attacks, often accusing Republicans of corruption. And some Democrats have imitated the president’s crude approach: Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, for example, made social-media posts this year suggesting that various conservatives were gay.

But in the midterms the Republican attacks stand out for their viciousness.

American political campaigns have long been awash in negative and dubious attacks by both parties — in debate lines, TV commercials and stump speeches — but this bitter, hard-fought cycle may set a new standard. Some political scientists said this election season had devolved into the most negative, dark campaign in modern American history.

“I think it’s the worst,” said Christina Greer, a political science professor at Fordham University. She attributed the tone to candidates’ desire to package their message for social media, and to Republicans’ mirroring of Mr. Trump: “He’s opened a portal to the degradation of our electoral system.”

In Texas, Vice President JD Vance suggested at a rally that Mr. Talarico was gay, drawing gasps from the crowd. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Mr. Vance added, referring to Mr. Talarico’s past statements in support of transgender youth.

Mr. Talarico has a girlfriend. The attack was part of a broad effort by Republicans to portray Mr. Talarico as extreme. Mr. Trump has taken to referring to Mr. Talarico as “Talafreako.”

A spokeswoman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee suggested that Democrats had brought the attacks upon themselves. In a statement, the spokeswoman, Bernadette Breslin, claimed that Dr. El-Sayed had “pledged support” for a terrorist regime and said that “if Talarico didn’t want to be called anti-meat, he shouldn’t have announced his campaign would go vegan.”

Dr. El-Sayed has said he is loyal to the U.S. Constitution. Mr. Talarico has said he is not a vegan and that his campaign “basically” runs on barbecue.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Flake said the coarseness of some Republican attacks stemmed from a mix of desperation in the party and a mimicking of Mr. Trump. But he said he found a “silver lining” in the backlash some of Mr. Trump’s “imitators” had experienced — including in Republican criticism of a headline-grabbing attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race.

That ad came from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor. The commercial featured the mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, who says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling,” even as Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance defended it.

Former President Barack Obama, appearing at a rally in Ohio this month, said he was baffled that “the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a Republican who built a brand on civility, denounced a radio ad from the top super PAC for Senate Republicans that cast her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, as a “freak” for having two children with his second cousin. Ms. Collins called for the ad to be taken down.

But Ms. Collins, who has deplored Mr. Jackson’s efforts to cast her as corrupt, herself commented on Mr. Jackson’s family in the summer, telling Politico: “I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin.”

Other Republican attacks have gone largely unchallenged inside the party. After Mr. Marshall suggested his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, was a “groomer” of children, there was no significant Republican criticism. And there was no Republican uproar after Mr. Trump used an anti-trans slur to refer to the Democratic Senate nominee in South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews, calling her “Tranny Annie.” (Dr. Andrews is not transgender.)

A spokesman for Mr. Hamilton, Tyson Brody, said in a statement that Mr. Marshall was “resorting to increasingly unhinged and inexplicable smears.” Dr. Andrews released an ad this month in which she said she did not support transgender women playing in women’s sports or gender transition surgeries for minors. (In 2022 she had spoken out against a trans sports ban in South Carolina.)

On the campaign trail in Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate, has often brought supporters who have questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to America.

At a Rogers rally in Plainwell, Mich., on Thursday, Senator Tim Sheehy, Republican of Montana, told the crowd, “You better be afraid,” suggesting that supporting Dr. El-Sayed would be a step toward Shariah law in Michigan. “We have a radical Islamist on the other side of this ticket who hates this country.”

Asked later about Mr. Sheehy’s comments, Mr. Rogers told reporters, “You haven’t heard me say any of those things.”

Dr. El-Sayed said at a rally on Sunday that Mr. Rogers’s “whole campaign is to point at me and my name and my faith.”

“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Islamophobic attacks have long been a feature of American politics. But in the past, candidates in both parties sought to push back. In 2008, the Republican nominee for president, Senator John McCain, defended his opponent, Barack Obama, when a woman at a rally said she did not trust him because “he’s an Arab.” Mr. McCain replied, “No, ma’am, he’s a decent family man.”

This year, Democrats say they fear that Islamophobic attacks on Dr. El-Sayed have resonated with some voters and are hurting his chances in a race that is critical in the battle for Senate control.

“I won’t say it’s the worst and most horrific ever,” Mike McGuinness, the Democratic mayor of Pontiac, Mich., said of the Republican attacks on Dr. El-Sayed’s faith and background. “But it is definitely a Hall of Fame contender.”

The Rev. Horace Sheffield III of New Destiny Christian Fellowship in Detroit said the rhetoric in the campaign felt to him as if it came from long ago in American history.

“This tenor and tone that we find ourselves in now is very dangerous,” said Mr. Sheffield, who supports Dr. El-Sayed and whose daughter is Mayor Mary Sheffield of Detroit. “And it’s all based on prejudice.”

Cayce Myers, a professor of political communication at Virginia Tech who studies negative ads, said the race in Michigan was a “test case” for how inflammatory a message could be and still help, rather than hurt, a candidate in 2026.

Negative ads typically are the most motivating, he said, and Republicans in Michigan and elsewhere appeared to be betting that their approach would help activate base voters more than it would alienate voters in the middle.

But, Professor Myers added, Republicans are “pushing up against the limit of what voters and the electorate have an appetite for.”

item.title: Talarico Makes Final Pitch to Texans: ‘You Are My Slingshot’
item.description:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, invoked the mythological grandness of his native state when he told a crowd in El Paso this week, “Our musicians are so iconic, they only need one name: Willie. Beyoncé. Selena.”

Improbable as it might seem, the once-obscure 37-year-old state representative and former middle-school teacher with the choirboy face has entered an elite pantheon himself.

A little more than a year after Mr. Talarico began his candidacy, he has become a marquee political persona, and not just in Texas. His race, which could become the most expensive in the history of nonpresidential campaigns, may well decide which party controls the Senate.

The Democratic candidate’s celebrity has thrown Republicans into a panic, prompting the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to donate an unheard-of $158 million to groups that support Mr. Talarico’s G.O.P. opponent and the state attorney general, Ken Paxton.

A smooth orator and prolific fund-raiser, Mr. Talarico has cast his upstart campaign in biblical terms. He is David, the corrupt political system exemplified by Mr. Paxton is Goliath and in whatever city he happens to be in, he declares, “You are my slingshot.” He has run a largely mistake-free campaign, although the flu took him off the trail for nine days.

He has consistently drawn overflow crowds, many of whom wear T-shirts declaring themselves to be “Talafreakos,” first deployed by Mr. Paxton as a term of derision. Last Tuesday, an estimated 4,000 people turned out in Lubbock — an extraordinary number for a Democrat in the ruby-red city — while Mr. Paxton was campaigning with President Trump less than three miles down the road.

In Texas, these count as remarkable feats for a Democrat. But because it is Texas, such accomplishments may still not be enough for victory.

“I think James has at most a 50 percent chance of winning,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party. “Which, look, in Texas, that’s phenomenal. If you told me a year ago a Democrat would have a coin-flip chance of winning, I’d be doing backflips.”

People close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign privately echoed Mr. Warford’s assessment of the race. A New York Times/Siena University poll in September and a CNN/SSRS poll conducted Oct. 20 to 27 showed Mr. Talarico ahead by 6 percentage points, but other recent public surveys show him either tied with Mr. Paxton or within the margin of error with a 2-point lead. The candidate’s internal polls match those tighter surveys, people close to Mr. Talarico said, and may not be fully capturing the sentiments of rural conservative voters who support Mr. Trump.

There is plentiful evidence the race could go either way. During the homestretch of Mr. Talarico’s campaign, from deep-blue regions (San Antonio, Laredo, the Rio Grande Valley and El Paso) to steadfastly Republican terrain (Midland and Lubbock), Mr. Talarico’s bursting-to-capacity crowds made it possible to imagine that he could flip a statewide race for the first time in decades. Just as ubiquitous were signs his efforts could fall short.

A major obstacle facing Mr. Talarico is the avalanche of attack ads funded by Mr. Musk, in which the candidate is portrayed as a far-left extremist. At a stop one afternoon at the Bexar County Democratic Party headquarters in San Antonio, Mr. Talarico assured volunteers that their door-knocking work would surmount Mr. Musk’s efforts, saying, “The political science is very clear: TV ads don’t make much of a difference.”

But three days later, one of Mr. Talarico’s supporters who attended the Lubbock event, Rebecca Murrow, begged to differ when a reporter asked whether the attack ads were having an impact among people she knew. “Oh, you better believe they are,” she said.

A friend standing next to her, Luke Anderson, concurred, citing his mother as one example of a person who could not bring herself to support Mr. Talarico after viewing the ads.

Still, Ms. Morrow added, “It makes me proud to be supporting someone who’s trying to change their minds, no matter how hard it is.”

Mr. Talarico’s barnstorming tour, “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts,” is named after part of the motto of the film and TV series “Friday Night Lights,” about Texas high school football. The candidate frequently recites the lyrics of Lyle Lovett, the Texas singer-songwriter. His omnipresent footwear is not-too-shiny Lucchese cowboy boots, primarily made in El Paso. In short, Mr. Talarico has made one thing abundantly clear in every campaign appearance: He really wants you to know that he’s a Texan.

Flashing his Lone Star credentials as an eighth-generation native son is a tacit acknowledgment that the pale and slightly built pastor-in-training does not personify the Texas swagger the way the state’s political titans of yesteryear did, among them former Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson and George W. Bush and former Govs. Ann Richards and Rick Perry. (As it happens, Mr. Paxton was born in North Dakota and spent some of his youth in California, though his party does not seem to hold that against him.)

The “I’m one of y’all” references also constitute a self-normalizing effort to make up for what Mr. Talarico now terms “cringey” remarks he uttered several years ago about God being “nonbinary” and his belief that there are six biological sexes.

While those earlier statements live on in attack ads, Mr. Talarico has provided little in the way of new material for his opponent’s ad makers. He is self-disciplined, stays on script and comes off as more the seminary student he once was than the kind of fire-breathing populist fashionable in the Trump era. He wears the same youthful, Texas business casual uniform every day: a tailored blazer, a crisp white dress shirt, jeans and those cowboy boots.

Although he talks to the local media, of late he has declined most interviews with the national press, including The New York Times, on the grounds that those engagements are less likely to win votes. He travels aboard his “Talarico for Texas” R.V. with a small inner circle of young aides rather than outside political consultants. At events, his volunteers distribute signs that have his name on one side and “Love Thy Neighbor” on the other.

Projecting himself as a conciliator has helped win support from more than two dozen current or former state Republican officeholders, not to mention two relatives of Mr. Bush: his brother Neil and his daughter Barbara. A source close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign confirmed that members of the family had reached out and that the candidate has been in touch with them. That said, the Bush name no longer means what it used to in Texas, and it remains to be seen if Mr. Talarico’s throwback appeal for a kinder, gentler political culture can prevail amid a pugilistic zeitgeist.

Mr. Talarico’s trip to Lubbock pointed to the subtext of his campaign. No matter what the polls say, in Texas the underdog is by nature the Democrat. Mr. Talarico does not have the luxury of focusing his efforts on the deep-blue urban areas of the state. He is obliged to find votes everywhere he can, even in hostile territory.

In both Midland and Lubbock, Mr. Talarico’s advance staff had to scramble to find bigger places that would accommodate his crowds, then made sure to post those images on social media. Talafreakos living outside Texas contrasted what they saw with Mr. Paxton’s lackluster gatherings and asked the inevitable question: With these crowds, how can we possibly lose?

Few if any of the roughly 600 Midland Democrats standing in line for Mr. Talarico’s event suffered any such illusions. “Our Talarico lawn sign is the only one for blocks around,” said Linda Jordan, 78, a Democrat. “The neighbors don’t talk to us much.”

Tamara, a 43-year-old Midland Democrat who declined to give her last name, said of her neighbors that “there’s no changing their minds” and that her energies were instead focused on persuading her husband to vote for Mr. Talarico. She suspected, she said, that he had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, though “he still won’t tell me.”

Mr. Talarico’s allies acknowledge that for him to win, he will need to maximize turnout in Latino-heavy communities. But Democratic Party officials said in interviews that while knocking on doors in both San Antonio and El Paso, they encountered abiding loyalty to Mr. Trump and an aversion to Mr. Talarico, particularly among Latino men. In downtown Lubbock this week, a long line of the president’s supporters waiting to get into a Trump rally included numerous Latino men, many of them wearing “Make America Great Again” caps.

Mr. Talarico’s surrogates are now couching their sense of urgency about the Latino vote in comic appeals.

In San Antonio, the actress Eva Longoria exclaimed: “Tell everyone! Tell your ex-boyfriend!” In El Paso, the city’s congresswoman, Veronica Escobar, beseeched a group of volunteer canvassers, “By all means, harass your family and your friends.”

In the end, people close to Mr. Talarico acknowledge that though Mr. Trump’s popularity has waned in Texas over the past two years, enough of his supporters remain to determine the outcome in Mr. Paxton’s favor, assuming they choose to back him.

In a last-ditch effort to split Republican loyalties, the Talarico campaign recently authorized the state party to send out mailers featuring a quote from a Texas woman: “I voted for Trump, but I cannot vote for Ken Paxton.”

Standing in line while awaiting Mr. Talarico’s arrival in Midland, Javier Soto, 59, said his father was among the many Texans who had supported Mr. Trump throughout the years. “But he says it’s time for a change,” Mr. Soto said.

item.title: Advocacy Groups Sue to Stop Trump Effort to Set Aside Ballots in Washington State
item.description:
Immigrant advocacy groups in Washington State filed suit late Friday night seeking to bar the Trump administration from forcing state election officials to set aside ballots from nearly 400 residents the administration believes may not be citizens.

The lawsuit, filed in Federal District Court in Seattle, was the latest legal move taken to stave off pressure from the White House to stop noncitizens from voting — even though the administration has often been wrong about whether registered voters are citizens.

The suit in Seattle came in response to a letter that federal prosecutors sent on Monday to Washington’s secretary of state, Steve Hobbs, demanding that he instruct election officials not to accept ballots from the 400 people until federal agencies could determine their citizenship.

Days later, Trent McCotter, the No. 2 official in the Justice Department, followed up with a second letter reminding Mr. Hobbs that mishandling ballots is a federal crime.

The suit from the advocacy groups took issue with both the accuracy of the list of voters sent to Mr. Hobbs and what it characterized as veiled threats of prosecution by senior Justice Department officials.

“Defendants’ list is not evidence of anything,” the suit maintained, “and their deeply chilling threats of federal penalty for election officials and others who fail to conform to their demands are baseless.”

Washington is not the only state that has faced heavy pressure from the Trump administration to set aside ballots from voters deemed to be ineligible because of their citizenship.

The administration sued California state officials, seeking to force them to set aside the ballots of more than 20,000 registered voters it said were noncitizens. That move was blocked for the second time on Friday by a federal appeals court, which determined that granting the government’s request would have undermined California’s authority over its election procedures and violated the “plain text” of the Constitution.

In a parallel effort, the Justice Department has issued a flurry of subpoenas to California state election officials in a widening criminal investigation seeking to prove its unsubstantiated claims that thousands of noncitizens are on California’s voter rolls.

But, in a major setback to the administration, a federal judge in San Francisco issued a ruling late on Friday blocking the Justice Department from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with its directives on handling ballots.

The ruling, by Judge Trina L. Thompson, ordered the department not to “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots” based on the government’s suspicion that the voters might be noncitizens. She has scheduled a hearing for Monday.

item.title: Susan Collins Is Always Keeping Score
item.description:
Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. He met with Mayor Carl Sheline, a fellow Democrat, in his office and over drinks at a local Italian restaurant. They had a series of phone calls. But ultimately Mr. Sheline declined to back him.

Ms. Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent, was not in the room, at the bar, or on the line.

But she had made her presence known.

Mr. Sheline had various reasons for withholding his support, he said in an interview. Among them, he acknowledged, were a housing project, a food distribution center, and a mill museum in Lewiston. Ms. Collins had helped with the finances for all of them.

“It’s just an environment of possible retribution,” Mr. Wood said. “It is that fear she instills.”

Over nearly 30 years, Ms. Collins, a self-styled moderate in a familiar Maine mold, has cultivated a public persona as a workhorse and a fastidious maestro of constituent services and pork-barrel disbursements, using her Washington know-how to get her constituents what they need.

But for just as long, her detractors say, she has managed to mostly mask another reality. “The gentlewoman from Maine,” as her colleagues say on the Senate floor, is a formidable power broker who can play a fierce brand of politics with a how-dare-you air. According to more than 40 interviews with Republicans and Democrats in Maine politics, former staff, colleagues and longtime observers, Ms. Collins has wielded power not so much as a Yankee Republican but as a shrewd machine politician.

“It’s almost like Tammany Hall,” said Amy Fried, a retired political scientist from the University of Maine. “You’re going to get this benefit here if you vote for me.”

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former aide to Ms. Collins, did not disagree.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said. “She’s openly discussing the fact that Maine is going to be set back if she’s not in that position,” he added. “It puts people in the position of very clearly understanding that voting against her is a vote against their own well-being.”

Ms. Collins’s staff stresses that she has worked to bring money back to all communities in Maine — regardless of whether they support her.

Annie Clark, a longtime aide to Ms. Collins, provided The New York Times an exhaustive list of projects, from Orono and Ogunquit to Belfast and Blue Hill, for which the senator had secured funding since 2021. The senator got $234 million for 96 projects in Cumberland and Knox counties — the only two counties she lost in 2020. In Portland, where she received just 21 percent of the vote: $51.2 million for 28 projects.

“Senator Collins has been extraordinarily effective,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins. “She works tirelessly to deliver results for the state, meets with thousands of Mainers every year, and she secures billions of dollars for communities in all of Maine’s 16 counties whether they vote for her or not.”

Ms. Collins, 73, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for re-election this fall the way she always has — no clickbait TikTok posts or big, rah-rah rallies, but a relentless focus on stops in small towns where she has brought home federal dollars for boat landings, emergency operations centers and wastewater treatment facilities.

At her campaign events, supporters hold signs that underscore the point she is trying to make: “Thank You, Susan.”

In debates this month with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, Ms. Collins was unsubtle about the crux of the deal.

“In the past five years I’ve secured $1.5 billion for properties all over the state,” she said.

She was even more blunt in a radio interview this week, citing 672 projects that she had secured across the state, including 45 new fire stations.

“All that goes away,” she said, “if Troy were to be elected.”

Her whole life has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power.

Ms. Collins was born and raised in Caribou in Aroostook County, the state’s most northern terrain. The Collinses didn’t just own and run the local lumber company and hardware store. They were politicos too.

“My parents,” Ms. Collins told The New York Times this past summer, “both served as mayor of Caribou. My father was in the State Senate, my grandfather, great-grandfather served in the state legislature.”

Her parents were supporters of William S. Cohen when he ran for Congress in 1972 and beyond, and Ms. Collins was a driver and an intern for Mr. Cohen when she was in college at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N.Y. After she graduated, she was hired as an aide and was on his staff for a dozen years, known by her colleagues and peers as a meticulous note-taker and over-preparer.

She ran for governor in 1994 when she was 41 and lost. She ran for Senate in 1996 and won. She said she would serve no more than two terms but then ran for re-election in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020.

Over the course of her three decades in the Senate, drafting off the renown of her cordial, consensus-building Maine forebears like Mr. Cohen and Senator George Mitchell, Ms. Collins has emphasized her image as the last of a vanishing breed. She has bucked her party, and in particular President Trump, more than enough to frustrate many Republicans — albeit not nearly enough to satisfy most Democrats.

“I’m consistently sought out by both sides for cosponsorship of bills,” she told The Times in her first year in the Senate. “I have a lot of power — I like that.”

Behind closed doors, though, she long has had a reputation as a lone wolf.

Her relationship with Olympia Snowe, the Republican who was elected to the Senate from Maine two years before Ms. Collins and served three terms, was marked by rivalries and perceived slights, according to former aides to Maine lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Publicly, they issued joint statements and often voted together. Privately, the relationship was far more fraught, as is sometimes the case when a state is represented by two senators of the same party.

“She was just hypersensitive to Olympia getting more credit than she was,” said Kurt Bardella, a former press secretary for Ms. Snowe.

“It was very machine-politicky: ‘I am owed a certain level of stature and respect,’” Mr. Bardella recalled.

Ms. Collins has a bristly relationship with Angus King, the independent junior senator from Maine, who defeated her in the governor’s race in 1994 and succeeded Ms. Snowe in 2013. While they exchange occasional text messages, the two haven’t spoken in months, according to people familiar with their communications who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. They last texted Oct. 12, according to Ms. Clark. Aides in Mr. King’s office often are instructed to let Ms. Collins get the lion’s share of the credit, they said, if that’s what it takes to get a policy initiative accomplished.

When Mr. Wood announced his candidacy for Senate, he thought he knew what he needed to know about Ms. Collins. His campaign quickly became a window into what he did not know.

Elected Democrats and political donors, Mr. Wood said, told him Ms. Collins reviewed the lists of who gives more than $1,000 to whom — and kept score.

“People told me they could not give me money because they knew she would look at the report,” he said. “Democrats.”

Ms. Clark, the spokeswoman for Ms. Collins, said the senator does not review such lists.

Ultimately, Mr. Wood’s fledgling campaign was overwhelmed by the unexpected rise of Graham Platner, whose subsequent fall precipitated Mr. Jackson’s selection as the Democratic nominee. Still, he got an eye-opening tutorial in the sway of his state’s senior senator.

Last November, when he ended his Senate campaign and switched to run instead for Maine’s Second Congressional District, Mr. Wood couldn’t help but notice the difference.

This time, Mr. Sheline, the Lewiston mayor, endorsed him right away.

This month, politicking her way through the annual fall fair in Fryeburg, Maine, Ms. Collins walked from a cattle auction to a livestock barn, putting up with out-of-town press asking her questions about the president while trying to steer clear of manure.

“I know you don’t like me,” she told one reporter, “but don’t make me walk through shit.”

She quickly changed the subject — to $38 million in federal aid for heating oil.

“I was delighted,” she said, “that I was successful in expediting the funding.”

That matters a lot, said Mr. Dutson, the senator’s former aide.

“Federal money is incredibly important up here,” he said. “The choice a lot of people are facing right now is: OK, well, I can listen to the noise out of Washington or what my party tells me to do — or I can support the lady who got me a new fire truck in my 500-person town.”

In the past few weeks in Maine, as Mr. Jackson has campaigned in front of large, loud crowds alongside progressive megastars such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ms. Collins has brandished a shovel at a groundbreaking at a boat landing in Orrington and attended a grand opening of a wastewater facility in Windham.

And in the stretch run of the race, people all over the state have received targeted text messages from her campaign.

“Susan Collins delivered $33 million for Knox County …”

“Susan Collins has delivered nearly $59 million for the City of Bangor …”

“Susan Collins is delivering real results across Kennebec County — 50 projects totaling more than $109.3 million …”

Her supporters say it’s why they trust her and one of the main reasons she should be re-elected.

“What she produces is real — it’s tactile,” said Chris Gardner, the executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, who has appeared in an ad for Ms. Collins. “We should be thankful.”

Kevin Raye, a former Maine Senate president and Ms. Snowe’s former longtime chief of staff, is an anti-Trump former Republican who is now an independent — “rooting,” he said, for Democrats to take control of Congress. “But I’m in the Collins camp,” Mr. Raye said, citing her record of bipartisanship. “The thought of replacing her with a reliable partisan vote, no matter the party,” he said, “is so the wrong direction for America.”

But the calculation, her critics counter, is more complicated. Her vote to advance Mr. Trump’s big domestic policy bill before she ultimately voted against it, her initial votes against setting congressional limits to military actions in Iran followed by eventual votes to do just that — all of it costs her constituents, they say, contributing to cuts to health care and higher prices for fuel, food and more. Many remain furious about her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, a move that ultimately led to the end of Roe v. Wade.

“She’s very good at cutting ribbons,” said Betsy Sweet, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and for Senate in 2020 against Ms. Collins. “She’s also really good at cutting your health care.”

Moreover, as she works to fend off her challenger in a tough year for Republicans, Ms. Collins’s sharp political style has been apparent not just to political insiders but to voters as well.

In a recent interview with Politico, Ms. Collins was startlingly cutting about her opponent.

“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” she said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.” They did now.

“This is a Susan people haven’t seen,” said Tony Payne, the executive director of the Republican Party of Maine in the 1970s who became an independent after the rise of Mr. Trump and a longtime critic of Ms. Collins. “This is the peeling off of the veneer.”

Last week, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the Republican Party’s candidates, aired a radio ad about Mr. Jackson with a crude jingle alluding to the relationship. After it had made the rounds, Ms. Collins told reporters she “had nothing to do with that ad,” saying it should be removed from the air.

This week, Ms. Collins’s campaign has been airing a TV ad that many in Maine considered elitist. “We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Bill Green, a well-known, retired local sportscaster, says in the ad.

“For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance,” Sam Patten wrote in a post on social media castigating the ad. (Mr. Patten, a former aide to Ms. Collins, pleaded guilty during the first Trump administration to failing to register as a foreign agent.)

“She’s very smart, and she works very hard,” Mr. Patten told The Times. “There’s an arrogance in everyone in Washington,” he added, “but she never showed it before. She’s always been careful not to.”

Ted O’Meara, a former aide to Ms. Snowe who also worked for Mr. Cohen alongside Ms. Collins and managed Eliot Cutler’s campaigns for governor in 2010 and 2014, described it as a sense of entitlement. “The sense that there’s nobody else that can do this job but me or do it as well as me,” he said.

He stopped himself.

“Is this on the record?” he asked.

It was.

“She’ll be pissed,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research. Tim Balk contributed reporting from Fryeburg, Maine, and Esmé E. Deprez from Caribou and Casco, Maine.

item.title: Shooting at Spirit Halloween in California Leaves at Least One Dead
item.description:
The police are searching for a person who shot and killed a pregnant mother of four and injured six others at a Spirit Halloween in Northern California on Friday evening, the local authorities said.

The shooting, which has rattled community members, occurred as shoppers clamored for last-minute costumes on the night before Halloween. A shooter opened fire inside the holiday store at the Solano Town Center mall in Fairfield, Calif.

When police officers arrived they found seven victims with gunshot wounds, the authorities said.

Constance Hages, 31, died from her injuries, Fairfield police said in a statement on Saturday afternoon. She was pregnant, her family told detectives.

Two of Ms. Hages’s relatives, Chelaya Colbert and Charmaine Colbert, said in phone interviews that Ms. Hages had four children and had previously worked at San Francisco International Airport.

Chelaya Colbert also said Ms. Hages, her cousin, was pregnant when she died.

“I’d like to remember her as the happy lady she was,” Chelaya Colbert, who is 25 and lives in San Francisco, said. “She loved her kids.”

Ms. Hages’s mother, Capricia Colbert, declined to speak when reached by phone, asking to be left alone to grieve her daughter.

Three other victims, including two teenagers, remained in critical condition. An additional victim is in critical but stable condition, according to the police. Two other victims were treated for gunshot wounds and have since been released from the hospital.

Janet Jacobo, 36, was shopping for a costume with her three sons, ages 6, 11 and 13, on Friday evening when she heard noises she believed to be gunshots, she said in a phone interview on Saturday.

Ms. Jacobo, who lives in Fairfield, Calif., told her children to run and began searching for an exit, she said. The doors between the mall’s interior and the Halloween store were already closed for the evening she said, adding that another shopper was rallying people to break the gate open so they could get out of the store.

She fled, running alongside her elder sons and carrying her youngest child who she said was “terrified.” As they ran, she said she heard a woman scream.

The Fairfield police did not offer any information about the identity of the victims or the potential suspect in what it called a “heartbreaking incident.” Police officials declined to answer additional questions when reached for comment, but said the police were working to confirm new details about the shooting.

“This is still a very active crime scene,” the statement said. “Detectives are speaking with witnesses and diligently working to identify the suspect responsible for this horrific shooting.”

The shooting appeared to have “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect inside the Spirit Halloween store,” Fairfield police said in a statement on Saturday, adding that they were encouraging people in the area to “remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”

The store remains closed, Lori Tesoro, a spokeswoman for Spirit Halloween said in an email on Saturday evening, adding that Spirit Halloween was cooperating with local law enforcement officials in the ongoing investigation.

Ms. Jacobo, who witnessed the shooting with her children, said she no longer plans to hand out candy this evening. She has tried to calm her six-year-old son by telling him the shooting was just a “scary show at the Halloween store.”

There was also a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Madison Heights, Mich., earlier on Friday. A 21-year-old man shot another 21-year-old man multiple times in a “brief altercation” at the holiday store in the Detroit suburbs, Madison Heights police said in a statement.

The victim, who lived in Detroit, was taken to a hospital with serious injuries and later died. The two men were acquainted, the police said in the statement. The police declined to answer further questions about the episode. The suspect in the Michigan shooting is in custody.

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Trump’s Arch Faces New Legal Challenge From Virginia and D.C.
item.description:
The District of Columbia and Virginia on Saturday sued the Trump administration to block construction of the president’s planned 250-foot arch, which he wants to begin building as early as next week.

“This project is flagrantly unlawful,” the lawsuit states.

The suit accuses the Trump administration of violating the Commemorative Works Act and a section of federal law that requires the federal government to obtain specific congressional authorization before building a monument on federal land in Washington.

The plaintiffs cite the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act, which require a process of consultation and considering alternatives before rushing forward with the project. The suit also says plans for the arch violate the Height of Buildings Act, which with limited exceptions prohibits structures taller than 130 feet in the capital.

“In their rush to break ground on the arch, defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the suit states. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”

The suit was filed by Jay Jones, Virginia’s attorney general, and Brian L. Schwalb, Washington’s attorney general.

It is one of several challenging the legality of President Trump’s arch, which the president has said is for himself but top administration officials now also claim is necessary for national security.

Arlington County, which borders the site of the planned arch, also has sued, citing traffic and safety concerns. A group of Vietnam War veterans also has sued to stop construction of the arch, which would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery from the Lincoln Memorial. That lawsuit also claims the project is unconstitutional without approval from Congress.

In a statement on Saturday, a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, did not respond to the claims in the latest suit but said the arch would serve as a landmark and “gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen and all Americans alike.”

A federal judge hearing the veterans suit expressed skepticism Friday over the Trump administration’s new argument that the president’s planned 250-foot triumphal arch is needed for national security purposes.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, contended in sworn statements that even though national security was never invoked in the initial proposal for the arch, the project was now needed to keep the United States safe from drone attacks.

But on Friday, Judge Tanya S. Chutkan of Federal District Court in Washington questioned what she called the “brand-new” national security justification.

“I’m wondering about the timing of this argument,” Judge Chutkan said, before asking for more details about Mr. Trump’s plans for snipers, drones and ammunition to be stored at the arch.

“Can you give me some support?” she asked. “Can you show me any piece of paper?”

Robert N. Stander, a deputy assistant attorney general, said he could not.

The Trump administration has tried to get that suit dismissed by contending that the veterans group lacks standing.

One of the plaintiffs, Michael Lemmon, an Army veteran who served in Vietnam, testified Friday that the proposed arch, which he called a “monstrous edifice,” would interfere with the solemn way he experiences the Arlington cemetery.

The administration says the arch will be a tourist attraction, bringing up to 22,000 tourists a day to the area. Mr. Lemmon called that “disturbing and frankly disrespectful” to the families of those buried at the site.

“The pain is real for us veterans,” he testified.

In arguing that the veterans lack standing, lawyers for Mr. Trump pointed to a recent Supreme Court ruling that shot down a legal challenge to the luxury ballroom Mr. Trump is building on White House grounds after he demolished the building’s East Wing. The court ruled that the plaintiffs, a preservationist group chartered by Congress, did not have the legal grounds to sue because they were not directly harmed by the project.

The suit from the District of Columbia and Virginia appears to present different challenges for the administration by detailing a list of what they say are concrete harms from the arch’s construction. The suit cites traffic concerns and emergency response problems, as well as issues concerning the environment and historic preservation.

“The construction of the arch will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the district and Virginia,” the suit filed on Saturday states. “The arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the district has a statutory responsibility to protect. Both the construction of the arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions.”

Even so, the arch is slated to receive final approval next week from the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by allies of Mr. Trump’s. Administration officials have told one federal court that they could break ground on the project immediately after the vote of the planning commission.

item.title: Democrats File Suit Over Closed Polling Places in Rural Alaska
item.description:
As a Justice Department lawsuit challenging the presence of two U.S. Senate candidates named Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot plays out, Democrats have filed a lawsuit in Alaska accusing election officials of failing to properly operate at least 18 rural polling locations.

The complaint, filed Friday afternoon in Anchorage Superior Court, warns that several thousand voters across remote, predominantly Alaska Native communities face disenfranchisement in a state where elections are routinely decided by a few thousand or even a few hundred votes.

Given Alaska’s vast geography and the logistical hurdles voters in remote areas encounter, state law allows any qualified voter to request an absentee ballot and establishes an in-person absentee and early voting window beginning 15 days before Election Day.

In remote communities, the state relies on agreements with local municipal and tribal offices to host and staff sites where residents can cast absentee ballots in person.

The Democrats’ lawsuit alleges that state-advertised absentee-in-person voting sites across 18 rural communities either failed to open, opened late, maintained irregular hours or lacked ballots altogether. In some communities, local workers reportedly resigned without replacements, while others had not received ballots or were unaware they were supposed to host voting.

According to the complaint, some voters traveled to their designated voting location “by boat or by plane” only to be turned away.

State Senator Bill Wielechowski wrote the elections division earlier this month, noting the 18 precincts that hadn’t opened and asking for help.

In her response this week, the Alaska elections director, Carol Beecher, said 12 of the 18 sites had confirmed they were open, three had declined to open, and state officials were still trying to contact the remaining three. She emphasized the role local partners are supposed to play in rural voting, suggesting blame for the confusion about where and when to vote rested largely in the villages rather than the state elections office.

Some 82 percent of Alaska communities are not accessible by road, and the state elections office routinely struggles to ensure residents in farther-flung places can vote, with ballots sometimes arriving too late to be counted or polling sites never opening.

This time around, Democrats want the state elections office to make sure all remote polling sites are open and stay open until polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day. They also want the state to pay their attorney fees.

item.title: ‘Poop Water’ Churns a Local Election in Parched Arizona
item.description:
A ritzy Arizona enclave is facing water cuts, and the most divisive idea to offset them begins with millions of gallons of sewage. Call it affluent effluent.

The plan — which involves rigorously treating and purifying wastewater, then routing it straight to residential taps — has long been seen as critical for the future of Scottsdale, a city heavily reliant on the dwindling flow of the Colorado River.

But in recent months, Scottsdale’s wastewater recycling program has been sucked into a bitter political dispute, and its fate could hinge on the outcome of the city’s elections on Tuesday.

The Scottsdale City Council, where two seats are up for grabs, is nominally nonpartisan, but this year’s race may change the balance of power on water issues. Two candidates, both running on a right-wing platform, deride wastewater recycling as an unproven experiment. They call it “toilet to tap” or “poop water.”

A third challenger, who is backed by Democratic groups, argues that the science behind wastewater recycling is robust, citing expert support for a technology considered safe and reliable. His opponents, he says, are capitalizing on residents’ fears of contamination and downplaying the seriousness of Scottsdale’s looming water crisis.

“They’re using buzzwords and scare tactics,” Raoul Zubia, a retired banker, said of his conservative opponents, Michelle Ugenti-Rita, a former state senator, and Barry Graham, an incumbent council member.

The dispute offers a colorful preview of the ways water is becoming increasingly politicized as scarcity forces local officials across the West to make difficult decisions and embrace unconventional solutions.

Scottsdale, a city of 240,000 northeast of Phoenix, is famous for its green golf courses and red rock peaks. It is an upscale destination for bachelorette parties and bar crawls, spas and shopping malls. But in wonkier circles, the city is also known as a leader in water treatment and engineering.

Nearly all American drinking water comes from lakes, rivers, reservoirs or underground aquifers. But Scottsdale Water, a city-operated utility, has been purifying wastewater for decades through a process with many steps and even more syllables — ozonation, membrane ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis, ultraviolet photolysis. Scientists say the resulting product is among the cleanest water in the world.

The city currently sends much of the recycled water to about two dozen golf courses, which use it for irrigation. It pumps the remainder into an aquifer, where it is eventually drawn out as drinking water, a longstanding process known as indirect potable reuse.

City leaders wanted to go further, skipping the aquifer and mixing purified water with other sources before delivering it to residential taps. That’s known as direct potable reuse.

Only a few direct potable reuse facilities operate around the world, but more are in the works. Scottsdale’s would have been Arizona’s first.

But in June, with the state updating regulations and the issue turning partisan, the City Council froze funding for the project, even as neighboring Phoenix pushed forward.

Supporters were dismayed.

“You cannot choose ‘no water’ because you have unfounded fears about water quality,” said Kathryn Sorensen, a water policy expert at Arizona State University.

Ms. Ugenti-Rita would be the program’s most vocal critic if elected. The idea is “disgusting,” she said, and she is worried recycled water could make residents sick. She has also balked at the cost of infrastructure upgrades, which city staff recently estimated at more than $160 million.

“There’s a lot at stake,” Ms. Ugenti-Rita said. “We don’t want to be the next Flint, Mich. I don’t want short or long-term health effects. We have a reputation to consider.”

Mudslinging reached its peak ahead of the summer primary election, when Ms. Ugenti-Rita appeared in a social media video with the MAGA-aligned comedian Rob Schneider.

Mr. Schneider, who was in the “The Waterboy” and lives in Scottsdale, held a cup of liquid the color of a milky latte while criticizing “toilet to tap.” He referred to one of Ms. Ugenti-Rita’s primary opponents, Solange Whitehead, as “Sewage Solange.”

Ms. Whitehead, who grew up wanting to be a sewage engineer, was unfazed.

“I was pretty flattered,” Ms. Whitehead said as she sipped a pale ale made with Scottsdale’s recycled wastewater, part of a campaign to help the public overcome the “ick factor.”

Ms. Whitehead, an incumbent council member who ran on water issues, finished first in the July primary, securing another term on the board and avoiding a runoff on Tuesday. She said she was concerned that her opponents’ rhetoric will turn residents against a critical technology.

“When you rile up people against something, it spreads,” Ms. Whitehead said. “This is not a good time to politicize and to try to create distrust.”

At Scottsdale Water’s sprawling campus, Thyra Ryden-Diaz, the utility’s interim director, defended the wastewater recycling program and said sending treated water directly to taps would not differ much from what the city was already doing.

“All water is recycled,” Ms. Ryden-Diaz said. “I don’t think that people remember their third-grade water cycle graph.”

Still, she said, it would not be a panacea for Scottsdale because the city already reuses so much of its wastewater, and unless facilities are upgraded, there will not be much left to send to taps.

Scottsdale is not running out of water anytime soon, but surveys show Arizonans are concerned that state leaders aren’t doing enough to save their most precious resource. Max Vega, a 40-year-old who works in the mining industry, is one of them.

Drinking recycled wastewater “may disturb some people,” he said on a recent evening after walking his dog at a large Scottsdale desert preserve. “But if you do it the right way, under safe regulations, then so be it.”

For others, the idea is a harder sell. Corlan and Becky Fawcett, who were visiting Scottsdale for a conference, said knowing wastewater ran from their hotel faucet would not stop them from returning.

“But it might make me want to buy my water when I get here,” Mr. Fawcett said.

The couple, who live in Utah, another water-strapped state reliant on the Colorado River, acknowledged that such technology might someday come to their hometown.

“What’s the alternative?” Ms. Fawcett asked. “What’s the other option?”

item.title: El-Sayed Doesn’t Want Haley Stevens to Join Him at Sunday Event
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, said Saturday that he did not want Representative Haley Stevens, his former primary rival, to join him at a party unity event in Detroit on Sunday.

“I don’t want any distractions,” Dr. El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally in Sterling Heights, Mich., outside Detroit. He added, “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”

Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed, who have been publicly quarreling for days, were initially expected to attend the Sunday event together, part of an effort by Representatives Debbie Dingell of Michigan and James E. Clyburn of South Carolina to broker a peace between the feuding Democrats on the eve of a critical election.

It was not immediately clear if Ms. Stevens would abide by Dr. El-Sayed’s request that she stay away from the event.

Ms. Stevens, a centrist who lost to the progressive Dr. El-Sayed by less than a percentage point in a bitter August primary, had said late Friday that she had not been told that she was unwelcome at the event. She did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.

Mr. Clyburn said Saturday that he had “no idea” if Ms. Stevens would attend. An adviser to Mr. Clyburn, Antjuan Seawright, said Ms. Stevens was still invited, and rejected any notion that Dr. El-Sayed could pull her invitation.

“This is not Abdul’s event,” Mr. Seawright said Saturday afternoon, adding, “The invitation still stands.”

Ms. Dingell, who had said Friday that she had secured the participation of Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Stevens at the event, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

Politico previously reported that Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign did not want Ms. Stevens at its events.

Dr. El-Sayed did not say at the rally in Sterling Heights whether his campaign had relayed the request directly to Ms. Stevens.

A schedule for the Sunday event, at a church in the North End of Detroit, said that speakers would include Mr. Clyburn, Dr. El-Sayed and Mayor Mary Sheffield of Detroit. Their remarks were set to be followed by a march to the offices of the Detroit Election Department, the schedule said.

Ms. Stevens was not listed as a speaker, though there was no indication she had ever been expected to deliver remarks.

Opinion polls show that Dr. El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, are locked in a tight race that could determine control of the Senate.

Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed differ over their positions on Israel. Ms. Stevens is a strong supporter of the country, and Dr. El-Sayed is a fierce critic.

Their unusual clash has become a flashpoint in Democrats’ broader debate about Israel, and some Democrats are anxious that infighting in the final days of the race will damage Dr. El-Sayed’s chances.

His relationship with Ms. Stevens was not always so tense. Ms. Stevens quickly endorsed Dr. El-Sayed after the primary, pledging to campaign with him, and they appeared together at a unity breakfast two days after the primary.

But they have not been seen together in the final stretch of the race, and Ms. Stevens made a series of recent appearances on cable TV in which she criticized Dr. El-Sayed’s outreach to Black and Jewish voters, two groups that Mr. Rogers has aggressively courted.

Ms. Stevens said in an interview Friday that she had been set off by a moment in a debate this month in which Dr. El-Sayed declined to answer a question about whether Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States.

On Wednesday, Ms. Stevens said she would not campaign with Dr. El-Sayed again before the election, and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat, said he was backing Mr. Rogers, citing Dr. El-Sayed’s positions on Israel.

Ms. Dingell, frustrated by the intraparty conflict, said she reached out to the warring Democrats and Mr. Clyburn, one of the highest-ranking African Americans in Congress, and asked them to appear together. By Thursday night, Ms. Stevens was saying that she would join Dr. El-Sayed at the event on Sunday.

But the efforts to make peace crumbled Friday, after Ms. Stevens issued a statement calling on Dr. El-Sayed to apologize for comments he had made about Israel and to denounce an ad from an outside group that suggests U.S. aid to Israel was making life in America more expensive. (The ad shows a shopper telling a man not to buy eggs because “we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.”)

Dr. El-Sayed responded to Ms. Stevens’s statement with a statement of his own saying that she seemed “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” He called on her to “focus on the task at hand.”

On Saturday, Dr. El-Sayed told reporters that he did “not agree with the contents” of the ad from the outside group. But he also said she wanted to “talk about” issues that he did not want to focus on in the final days of the campaign.

As of Friday, Mr. Turkish said he planned to attend the church service.

On Saturday afternoon, he said he wanted to spend Sunday “however my fiancé, Haley, wants to spend her day.”

But, he added, he did not know if that would include the service.

item.title: Women Voters: The Silent Democratic Majority
item.description:
In the scramble to understand where America’s head is politically this election season, the focus has been on the working class, on Hispanics and on young men. But the country’s single biggest demographic group — women — is still the main driver of voting and in this election is looking more Democratic than ever.

Women have been the backbone of the Democratic base for decades and vote overwhelmingly for Democrats most years.

In 2022, support dipped slightly, when 48 percent of women chose Democrats and 41 percent supported Republicans. But this year, support looks set to return to more typical results, with 56 percent of women saying they prefer Democratic candidates, compared with 37 percent who say they prefer Republican ones, according to New York Times/Siena University surveys.

Women are a potent political force because they vote at higher rates than men.

And this year, they are bringing a lot of energy to volunteer and get-out-the-vote efforts.

Lynda Hoving, a retired appraiser and longtime volunteer for the Democratic Party in Kent County, Mich., has been sending postcards and working the phones for Democrats.

She watched as her West Michigan county, home to Gerald Ford and a tradition of Republicanism, went from solidly red in the 1970s, when she and her husband moved there, to reliably blue in more recent political cycles.

“I was always trying to turn something from red to purple,” said Ms. Hoving, who spent years in Grand Rapids stuffing envelopes, door-knocking and making spreadsheets. “It has been my goal for my whole political life.” She said it was disproportionately the women in the county who “kept the balls rolling” for the slow, tedious work of local politics.

Now 73, she said she still reminded everyone to vote during election season, including, most recently, her orthodontist, who told her he had voted for Trump but was not happy with the way things had turned out.

But she didn’t get to try to pitch him on Democrats.

“Then they put the plastic in my mouth, and I couldn’t talk anymore,” she said. “That’s one way to force a Democrat to listen.”

Pat Smithson, 69, of Lenexa, Kan., has volunteered so much for Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Kansas, that he called out her name when he walked into a campaign event on Saturday morning. She had brought cinnamon rolls freshly baked by her daughter.

Ms. Smithson, a retired fund-raiser, has been calling voters all over Kansas since June and said that even her daughter, a Republican who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, planned to vote for Mr. Hamilton, too. “She listened to him on TV,” Ms. Smithson said. “She watches me volunteer, setting the example.”

Some of the shift away from Republicans among women in recent years has been driven by Donald Trump.

Annette Hunt, 58, who works in finance and lives in Dallas, grew up in a staunchly Republican family in East Texas.

“Reagan was almost like a God in our house,” she said.

She said she voted straight ticket Republican for most of her life. Then came Mr. Trump.

She thought he would be “like Ross Perot — a businessman who shook up the Republican Party a bit,” but she couldn’t bring herself to vote for him, so she wrote in her father, who died that year. She has always regretted it, and ever since has voted Democratic to “stop the current agenda of the Republican Party.”

Last Saturday, she voted early for James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas. She said she did not feel at home in the Democratic Party either, despite voting for their candidates for the past 10 years.

“I’m a person without a party,” she said.

Jeanne Russell, 77, who owns a farm on Verona Island, Maine, said she grew up in a Republican household but was shaped by the politics that defined her young adulthood and ended up a liberal.

“I was a child of the ’60s and ’70s,” she said. “I was aware of the injustices in the country. It bothered me. So I’ve always been a Democrat.”

She said she has never missed an election.

Murray Carpenter contributed reporting.

item.title: Newsom Warns California’s Top Courts About Election Interference
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday warned the state’s top judges that the Trump administration may try to seize midterm election ballots as a legal battle continued over unproven federal claims that noncitizens are voting in huge numbers in California.

“I have grave concerns federal agents will seek search warrants to seize ballots and ballot materials before the election results are certified,” the governor wrote in an extraordinary “alert” to the four U.S. District Courts that cover California.

He added: “Indeed, the only reason to do so would be to interfere in a State’s lawful counting of ballots and certifying the results of the election.”

The warning came as the Trump administration is also claiming that there are more than 20,000 California voters who are “likely noncitizens" — an assertion that state election officials have firmly rejected.

On Saturday, data scientists analyzing that list of voters said in a court filing that it contains thousands of errors.

Mr. Newsom’s concerns about the seizure of voting machines or ballots are not unfounded.

In January, federal agents executed a search warrant at an election center in Fulton County, Ga., hauling away boxes of ballots in an effort to discredit Mr. Trump’s defeat in the 2020 election. The warrant in Fulton County was approved by a federal magistrate judge even though it was based on a series of debunked conspiracy theories about the contentious 2020 presidential race.

Ever since, election officials have worried that the Justice Department might try something similar in different jurisdictions, especially during the highly fraught days after the midterm elections.

Those concerns have not been assuaged, as Mr. Trump himself has warned that the country’s voting machines are vulnerable to foreign meddling. The president has also said that he regretted not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election.

Mr. Newsom is not the only public figure who has expressed concern that the Trump administration might resort to seizing ballots or voting machines.

On Tuesday, two former federal judges issued an unusual public statement to their working colleagues, warning them to use extreme caution before taking the “uniquely serious” step of granting prosecutors a warrant for seizures.

“Unlike the execution of a search warrant for contraband such as drugs or for the records of a criminal enterprise, executing a search warrant for ballots or voting machines before an election is certified would cause irreparable harm to a vital public process: our elections,” the former judges, J. Michael Luttig and Nancy Gertner, wrote.

Mr. Newsom’s letter to the judges was issued on the same day two data scientists from University of California, Los Angeles, released their findings of an analysis of the list of the 20,000 registered voters in California the Trump administration has claimed are not eligible to vote because they are not citizens.

The analysis — contained in court papers filed in district court in Washington by immigration advocates — found that more than 40 percent of the people on the list do not appear on the California state voter rolls. The analysis also found that the list contained thousands of people who appear to be citizens.

The scientists conducted their study by comparing the government’s list of suspected noncitizens with lists of people who had obtained citizenship. They did so with the help of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, a major California nonprofit colloquially known as CHIRLA.

The administration sued California seeking to force state officials to set aside any ballots cast by the 20,000 voters. But a federal appeals court has twice shot down that effort, saying it would rob the state of its authority to administer the election and violate the “plain text” of the Constitution. In between that court’s rulings, a district court in Los Angeles also rejected the administration’s request.

In his letter, Mr. Newsom wrote that, while he was not aware of any such pending application, “the tactics and rhetoric federal officials are using strongly suggest that, having lost repeatedly in federal civil proceedings thus far, they will quickly pivot to the criminal forum.”

The letter included a nonpartisan guide for evaluating search warrant applications that the judges could distribute to lower level federal magistrates.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed Does Not Want to Talk About Haley Stevens. Everyone Else Does.
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed had just finished his stump speech, complete with jokes about his name and exhortations to “show just how big we are” by turning out voters on Election Day. Then he walked into a room full of reporters wanting to ask about the one topic he wished not to discuss.

Representative Haley Stevens.

The first question came from a local reporter, who asked if Dr. El-Sayed believed Ms. Stevens, the congresswoman he defeated in the Senate primary who has been on a media tour criticizing his views on Israel, was trying to damage his campaign.

“That is not a question for me,” Dr. El-Sayed said, with a laugh that seemed to be a response to the crude term, including the word “rat,” that the questioner used to describe political sabotage.

The next question: Would Dr. El-Sayed do as Ms. Stevens demanded and disavow an online advertisement produced by one of Dr. El-Sayed’s allies blaming U.S. policy toward Israel for the price of groceries and health care?

Dr. El-Sayed was no longer amused.

“I’ve already been clear that that ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” he said.

He did not wish to talk more about Ms. Stevens. If the next question was about her or the ad she wished he’d disavow, Dr. El-Sayed said he would stop taking questions and walk out.

Throughout the 12 minutes he spoke with reporters, Dr. El-Sayed never said Ms. Stevens’s name. Once he referred to her as “the congresswoman.”

He fielded a few questions about the Detroit church service he planned to attend Sunday with Representative James E. Clyburn of South Carolina and his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers.

But soon he got back to Ms. Stevens.

Why, he was asked, shouldn’t he address the issues she raised, which are also of concern to some Michigan voters? Dr. El-Sayed said the primary was over.

“We had a primary, right? And the outcomes of the primary are what they were,” he said. “I understand that some folks are upset about that. I get it. But I’m here trying to beat Mike Rogers.”

Then: Did he still want Ms. Stevens to come to church with him Sunday, as his campaign first alerted Thursday and as she said Friday that she would?

Dr. El-Sayed said he did not want “distractions.” Ms. Stevens, he said, “wanted to talk about other things” beyond his campaign’s core themes.

Translation: She wants to talk about Israel and he does not.

Finally, Dr. El-Sayed was asked a version of the first question. Had Ms. Stevens hurt the Democratic ticket by speaking out against his campaign?

He said she does not matter, and that he does not think much about her.

“It’s not really of relevance to Michigan voters. Most people don’t care about this,” he said. “I just don’t spend much of my time thinking about these sort of personality issues. Like, I have much respect to the congresswoman. We had a hard-fought primary. That primary ended in August. I’m focused now on beating Mike Rogers.”

item.title: Centuries After Their Slaughter, Missionaries Move Toward Sainthood
item.description:
The Franciscan friars had left behind a world they had known in Spain for a new one across an ocean, dispatched to missions along the marshy coastline of what would one day become the state of Georgia. The men believed they had been sent there on an assignment handed down to them by God.

The missionaries learned the language of the Guale people, the region’s Indigenous inhabitants. The friars forged relationships, working to baptize them and bring them to Christianity, researchers found. But eventually, a rupture emerged. The teachings of this new faith collided with traditions that had existed long before these outsiders arrived. And in a bloody rampage, five of the Franciscans were killed.

More than 400 years later, the Catholic Church took a rare and sacred step to advance the friars toward sainthood. Decades of inquiry and deliberation culminated on Saturday when the church officially declared them as “blessed,” positioning them to join a cohort of roughly a dozen American saints and to possibly become the first connected to the South.

The friars — Pedro de Corpa, Blas Rodríguez de Cuacos, Miguel de Añon, Antonio de Badajoz and Francisco de Veráscola — had been forgotten for centuries by all but a few. But now, after the enduring efforts of fellow Franciscans and the Catholic community in South Georgia to revive their memories, the church has recognized them as martyrs, killed in defense of their faith.

“They reflect the light of Christ in the challenges and complexities of a wounded world,” Cardinal Frank Leo, the metropolitan archbishop of Toronto, told a crowd of thousands who had gathered for the beatification Mass he presided over in Savannah, Ga.

“They lived and labored, served and suffered so long ago,” Cardinal Leo added, and they were “now being raised at the glory of the altar.”

In the generations since the missionaries were killed, Christianity has flourished in Georgia. There are the many small towns where the steeples of Protestant churches seemingly rise above every block. Evangelical megachurches sprouted in the suburbs. Black congregations in Atlanta became the spiritual home of the civil rights movement.

Yet Catholicism has had a limited foothold. The charter establishing Georgia as a British colony specifically forbade the faith. These days, just 3 percent of the population in South Georgia identifies as Catholic, according to the local diocese.

Part of the jubilation now was a reassurance for the local Catholic community of how deep their roots run here, too.

“Often, we may be misunderstood,” the Most Rev. Stephen D. Parkes, the bishop of Savannah, said of Catholics in a place where Christians of other denominations could be skeptical of some of their traditions and practices, especially the veneration of saints. “It’s an opportunity for us to help spread the good news of the Catholic Church.”

Still, the legacy of the missionaries is also interwoven with a broader and darker history of conquering and conversion, with Native American groups saying the beatification was a reminder that the tragedies of that era were by no means limited to the deaths of the friars.

The descendants of Native Americans in Georgia were largely displaced from their ancestral homes. The Guale people no longer exist as a distinct group; some fled, some were killed and some were absorbed into other tribes, including the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, which was itself expelled from Georgia by the U.S. government two centuries later.

“The events of 1597 occurred during a complex and often violent period of Spanish colonization, when Indigenous peoples struggled to preserve their sovereignty, cultural traditions and ways of life,” RaeLynn A. Butler, the secretary of culture and humanities for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, said in a statement. “While the killing of the friars was tragic, the history of the Guale people extends far beyond those events and deserves to be understood in its own right.”

The service on Saturday was threaded with somber reflection, with acknowledgments of the discord and bloodshed that had brought the worshipers together. But the atmosphere was overwhelmingly one of joy.

A convention hall — a secular cathedral of gray and beige — was transformed by reverent pageantry.

A parade of dozens of bishops and priests, all in robes and vestments, processed nearly the length of the hall as organ music rumbled. Banners with images of the friars hung from the rafters. A makeshift altar was draped with marigold and maroon curtains.

The beatification comes at a moment of renewal and optimism for American Catholics as the church has tried to shake a cloud of scandal. The emergence of Pope Leo XIV, the first American pontiff, has helped inspire enthusiasm. Some of the country’s largest dioceses welcomed more converts into the faith this Easter than they have in more than a decade.

And in September, another American joined the ranks of the blessed: Some 50,000 people packed into a stadium in St. Louis for the beatification Mass of Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen, who became a household name as a missionary using mass media to draw thousands toward Catholicism.

By contrast, the Franciscan friars ministered on a much more modest scale, their lives and deaths largely obscured by history.

The bodies of the men were lost. The missions where they served had been reduced to archaeological ruins or had vanished altogether. But those who devoted years of their lives to pursue sainthood for the friars operated with a certainty that a solid-enough historical record had survived.

“This case, despite the amount of time it has taken, is really very simple,” the Rev. Conrad Harkins, the Franciscan who helped lead the effort before his death in 2020, told The Augusta Chronicle in 2007 as he prepared to travel to the Vatican with almost 500 pages of records.

“You’re either going to accept the historical documents,” he said, “or you’re not.”

Pope Francis certified their martyrdom last year, just a few months before his death. There is no definite timeline for when they might be canonized, the final step to attaining sainthood.

According to research compiled by the church, the friars had lived peacefully among the Guale, converting many within that community, including relatives of a local leader.

But the break came when the nephew of a Guale chieftain and his likely heir shared plans to marry a second wife, as had been custom. The Franciscans informed the man that doing so violated the faith he had been baptized into, and if he proceeded, the order would oppose his elevation to chief.

The man returned with other men and bludgeoned Pedro as he prepared for Mass. His severed head was impaled on a pike. The rampage continued, killing the other four friars and then holding and torturing another until his release was negotiated by the Spanish after 10 months.

Some scholars have argued that the men were killed as part of a broader power struggle. The church concluded through its investigation that the motivation had been religious, finding the friars had been killed “in hatred of the faith.” Some of the friars were even encouraged to flee, but they refused.

Church officials have presented them as defenders of marriage as a sacrament. If they proceed to full sainthood, the Rev. Roger Lopez, a leader in the Franciscan province for the United States, said he could imagine them as patrons for those who evangelize “the beauty of marriage.”

But Father Lopez also drew a more personal lesson from the friars’ experience. He, too, could be called to die for his faith, he said, and he needed to be prepared. It meant forgiving who he should forgive, making peace where it was needed and making sure those he loves knew of his love.

“I want to be ready, just like these brothers,” he said. “Not out of fear, but out of a sense of living a life that is whole, that is full.”
